title: Built-in strict CSP support in Next.js

events.summary: A contributor proposes making Next.js work under the strictest Content Security Policy by removing inline scripts and styles, moving server data into a JSON script tag, adding style nonces, and a contentSecurityPolicy config option that emits a header or meta tag.
A contributor asks whether another element could carry the app state, worrying some browsers treat a JSON script tag as inline script.
A contributor notes the change still adds an inline script, defeating the purpose.
A contributor wants the extra bootstrap request discussed first and would rather fold the code into an existing bundle.
The author replies that a JSON script tag is standard and CSP only governs executable JavaScript.
The author explains pages load asynchronously, so a small separate bootstrap file must run first.
The author argues the bootstrap file can be cached long-term, saving bytes overall, especially over HTTP/2.
The author repeats that non-JavaScript script tags are ignored by CSP.
The contributor doubts all browsers comply and suggests a data attribute on head instead.
The contributor points out the tag in question has no type attribute and asks whether a strict policy was tested.
The author says that inline script is temporary until webpack can define it.
The author cites Drupal using the same JSON technique.
The author retitles the PR around moving the inline script into a bootstrap file.
The author marks the PR ready for review.
A contributor calls recommending unsafe-inline a bad idea and suggests hashes for the remaining inline script.
A contributor says the test change weakens the existing policy and favours hashes or nonces.
A maintainer asks whether the bootstrap logic could live in the client entry.
A maintainer wonders whether a workaround is still needed with current webpack.
The author clarifies the unsafe-inline note concerns styles, which need special handling.
The author explains page registration functions must exist before any async page script loads.
The author says removing the workaround breaks everything.
The author shows the existing test policy already allowed inline styles.
The contributor concedes he misread the rule.
A contributor asks whether the extra script request was agreed or the code can be bundled.
A contributor asks for an example with a custom document and strict policy.
The author thinks an example is unnecessary since setup is now just a header.
The author says script order cannot be guaranteed and putting it in the webpack runtime was too complex.
The author plans automatic CSP support, including nonces for generated styles.
A maintainer clarifies he only meant reading the server data could move.
The author says the data is needed immediately afterwards.
A maintainer questions why the pathname is escaped separately.
The author marks the PR as work in progress again.
The author explains he escaped early to avoid bundling an escaping library.
The author notes a dependency on a styled-jsx nonce PR.
A maintainer asks to use nanoid instead of a just-removed package.
The author retitles the PR Strong CSP Support.
The author asks for review, saying unsafe-inline is no longer needed for styles and setup takes three lines of config.
A maintainer shares how to run single tests.
A maintainer asks to move nonce handling into render methods so custom servers also benefit.
A contributor asks whether the config also covers static exports.
The author says nonces cannot work for static pages since they are per request.
A contributor asks what a csp-nonce meta tag is for.
A contributor would prefer the config to cover static exports without a custom document.
The author says the meta tag passes the nonce to the CSS-in-JS library.
The author says static hosts must set the header themselves and allow inline styles or extract them.
The contributor notes most exporters use CDNs and asks for a meta tag emitted from config.
The author adds a config option to put the policy in a meta tag.
The contributor questions the unsafeCSPMeta name and proposes separate header and meta options.
The author defends the name because meta delivery is weaker than headers and says one policy suffices.
The contributor disagrees that meta delivery is unsafe and wants the config name to state the mechanism.
The author says he will document it in code instead.
A maintainer notes a stale name in the README.
The author explains flaky tests.
A maintainer links his PR removing module.exports from client bundles.
A maintainer says that PR fixes the bootstrap workaround.
The author notes a failing test until styled-jsx is released.
The author reports error pages are not processed by styled-jsx.
The author shows the warning and documents that CSP needs a custom error page.
The author says only a styled-jsx release is missing.
The author asks for a release, later noting it shipped.
The author adds a request for maintainer attention to the title.
A contributor warns that relaxing style and script rules in development but not production will cause confusing failures.
The author says hot reloading requires the relaxation and recommends testing production builds for violations.
The contributor traces eval to a DLL plugin and inline styles to the error overlay, and would rather disable the overlay than allow unsafe-inline in development.
The author asks for a fix and plans to extract the overlay's styles.
The author notes the overlay may run in an iframe.
The author removes the attention request from the title.
The author finds Proxy cannot be used because IE11 lacks it.
A contributor offers his Proxy shim.
The author declines a third-party shim in route loading and keeps an array push approach.
The contributor explains he removed the DLL plugin.
The contributor notes the overlay applies inline styles to the iframe itself.
The author plans to drop the DLL plugin, suggests a fix upstream in the overlay, and plans automatic policy generation.
The contributor asks a maintainer to confirm the plugin overlap and offers to help upstream.
The contributor finds the overlay also runs an inline script and that strict-dynamic in development helps.
The author prefers a proper overlay fix over strict-dynamic, which would diverge from production.
A contributor suggests a shorter README name.
A contributor notes Proxy breaks IE11.
The author links his earlier comment on that.
The author agrees and plans a README rewrite.
A maintainer links his PR removing registration code from initial markup.
A maintainer asks what a string replace is for.
A maintainer links his PR moving server data into a JSON script tag.
The author explains escaping only the closing script tag suffices for JSON and apologises for slow progress.
The author points to that explanation.
A maintainer says he kept the existing escaping and has already landed the JSON tag, route registration and error page parts, suggesting a fresh PR for the rest.
A contributor asks whether removing nonces breaks the strict CSP example.
The author says nonces are no longer needed for scripts and the example will become a config option.
The contributor asks whether third-party scripts must be allowlisted by domain and strict-dynamic is lost.
The author says allowlisting by domain is the point of CSP.
The contributor cites Google research recommending strict-dynamic over allowlists.
The author plans automatic allowlisting but finds the point interesting.
The contributor shares a talk and explains his stake, having contributed the strict-dynamic example.
The author notes strict-dynamic cannot work for static sites but agrees to keep the nonce option.
The contributor asks to keep both examples and notes scripts like tag managers defeat automatic allowlisting.
The author suggests automation be opt-in and hopes built-in support replaces the examples.
The author opens a PR upstream to stop the error overlay using inline styles.
The author argues allowlists better block rogue npm packages and suggests encouraging them where possible.
The contributor accepts the point and is glad both options stay.
A maintainer urges landing the PR soon.
A contributor asks whether the inline-script hash helper still works.
The author says inline scripts are gone so the helper is unnecessary, but keeps it to avoid a breaking change.
The contributor thanks him.
The contributor still sees script tags on canary.
The author says JSON script tags do not execute.
A maintainer asks the author to message him privately on Spectrum.
The author finds the error overlay's iframe script needs unsafe-inline and wonders about a custom Next.js overlay.
A maintainer tags the create-react-app maintainers.
A create-react-app maintainer offers to make the overlay CSP-compatible, dislikes the proposed upstream PR, and asks for a default-friendly approach.
The author explains the inline iframe styles and why a separate iframe page would be needed.
The overlay maintainer asks whether injected style tags or class names would work.
The author says styles must be external or nonce-tagged and inline scripts are harder.
The author builds a demo of a CSP-safe iframe setup and argues strict policy in development catches issues early.
A maintainer marks the PR as work in progress.
A user asks for an update.
A maintainer says it will not land before v8 and will be revisited later.
A user asks whether CSP can be added manually now that v8 removed inline JavaScript.
The author says production works but development still raises errors.
A maintainer closes the PR as outdated, noting the author has joined the Next.js team.
The PR is closed unmerged.
A user asks for the follow-up PR.
A user asks for news or docs.
A maintainer points to the strict CSP example and releases that removed inline JavaScript.
A user notes custom headers arrived in Next.js 9.5.
A user asks about nonce support for other CSS-in-JS libraries, which was never finished.
